summary: This RFC extends Virtual Private Wire Service bit-stream payloads beyond TDM signals, giving pseudowire transport with full signal transparency over packet switched networks. It allows a private line to be emulated across a packet network.

plainLanguage.summary: An old dedicated phone-style wire is pretended over a modern shared network. The signal comes out exactly as it went in.

questions: how to carry bit streams over a packet network
how does ple handle lost packets
subtitle: Carry a raw Ethernet, SONET/SDH, Fibre Channel or OTN signal across a packet network as if it were a dedicated line.

tldr.problem: Some customers need a physical-layer signal such as 10GBASE-R, Fibre Channel or SONET/SDH carried between two sites untouched, with its framing and timing intact. Frame-by-frame carrier services interpret the data and so cannot offer that.
tldr.mechanism: Private Line Emulation (PLE) chops the incoming bit-stream into fixed-size payloads and sends each one in a packet with a 4-byte control word and an RTP header, over an MPLS or SRv6 tunnel. The far end buffers the packets, replaces lost data and recovers the clock.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard with no obsoleting or updating RFC. It also defines new SRv6 behaviors and IANA assignments, including IP protocol number 147.

today: RFC 9801 was published in July 2025 as a Proposed Standard, and no RFC obsoletes or updates it. Signaling extensions for LDP and EVPN-VPWS are out of scope and are only mentioned as work in progress.

sections.title: Why Emulate a Private Line
sections.content:
RFC 9801 describes Private Line Emulation (PLE), a way to encapsulate bit-stream signals, not only Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) signals, as a Virtual Private Wire Service (VPWS) over a Packet Switched Network (PSN). It complements the structure-agnostic TDM method in RFC 4553 and widens it from the narrow set of PDH interfaces (T1, E1, T3, E3) to Ethernet, Fibre Channel, SONET/SDH and Optical Transport Network (OTN) signals at gigabit speeds.

The RFC gives three motivating cases. Two Ethernet devices may need Synchronous Ethernet to work end to end without the provider's equipment interfering. Two data centers may extend a storage network without touching the Fibre Channel protocol mechanisms. SONET/SDH add/drop multiplexers can be interconnected without the provider interfering with their multiplexing structures.

That last case is the key difference from Circuit Emulation over Packet in RFC 4842. PLE provides an independent layer network underneath the SONET/SDH layer network, whereas CEP operates at the same level and peers with it.
sections.plainLanguage: Some customers want their data to travel exactly as it left, like a sealed parcel. PLE carries the whole sealed parcel without opening it.

sections.title: Reference Model and Timing
sections.content:
Two Provider Edge (PE) routers each have an Interworking Function (IWF) that encapsulates the bit-stream into PLE packets and, in the other direction, rebuilds the bit-stream. In front of the IWF may sit a Native Service Processing (NSP) function from RFC 3985. It does service-specific work such as terminating FEC, terminating the OTUk layer for OTN, or handling multiple lanes. PLE follows the minimum intervention principle: data flows through the encapsulation layer as received, without modification.

Timing is carried across the network too. The local oscillators of both PEs are locked to a common clock. The difference between the attachment circuit clock and that common clock MUST be explicitly transferred from one PE to the other using the timestamp inside the RTP header, and the far PE regenerates the circuit clock by differential clock recovery. How the PEs lock to the common clock is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends are like walkie-talkies that must tick at the same speed. PLE writes down the tiny speed difference on every package so the far end can match it.

sections.title: Services PLE Can Emulate
sections.content:
The generic PLE service carries a bit-stream of any rate with no NSP function. The other services are special cases of the structured bit-stream from RFC 3985, and each one confines its specific handling to its NSP function.

  • Ethernet (1000BASE-X, 10GBASE-R, 25GBASE-R, 40GBASE-R, 50GBASE-R, 100GBASE-R, 200GBASE-R, 400GBASE-R): emulation works at the physical layer, specifically the PCS. Where an optional or mandatory FEC exists, the PSN-bound NSP MUST terminate it and the CE-bound NSP MUST generate it. Backplane PMD variants and interface types mandating auto-negotiation (except 1000BASE-X) are out of scope.
  • SONET/SDH: data is mapped into the payload with no awareness of frames; faults such as LOS, LOF and OOF are detected by the NSP.
  • Fibre Channel (1GFC to 64GFC): PLE works at the FC-1 layer, and speed negotiation is not supported.
  • OTN: the NSP terminates FEC and replaces the OTUk overhead in row 1, columns 8-14 with all zeros, giving an extended ODUk frame that is mapped into a byte-aligned payload.

For 200GBASE-R and 400GBASE-R, rate compensation blocks are inserted so the carried 66B stream runs at 528/544 of the nominal bitrate. Energy Efficient Ethernet deep sleep is not compatible with PLE, but fast wake mode is, so 25GBASE-R and higher can use LPI.
sections.plainLanguage: PLE can carry many kinds of cable signals. Each kind has a small helper at the edge that knows its quirks, and the middle part just carries the bits.

sections.title: The PLE Packet and Headers
sections.content:
A PLE packet has the PSN and VPWS demultiplexing headers, then the PLE header (a 4-byte control word followed immediately by a fixed-size RTP header), then the bit-stream payload. The total packet size for a pseudowire MUST NOT exceed the path MTU between the two PEs. The PSN layer can be MPLS or SRv6, and the RFC does not suggest a specific technology.

In the control word, the first nibble is 0000. L is set when the payload is invalid because of an attachment circuit fault, and the downstream PE MUST send replacement data. R is set by the downstream PE when it sees packet loss from the PSN or a server layer backward fault. RSV and FRG are zero because PLE does not fragment. LEN is always zero because no padding is added. The 16-bit sequence number is incremented with every packet sent.

The RTP header (from RFC 3550) is reused to convey timing. Version is 2, and P, X, CC and M are zero. The payload type comes from the dynamic range. The timestamp clock is 125 MHz for bit-streams up to 200 Gbps and 250 MHz above that. Full RTP features such as CSRC lists, RTCP and SRTP are not intended.
sections.plainLanguage: Each package gets a label with a number so they can be put in order, two warning flags to say something went wrong, and a clock stamp so the far end can keep time.

sections.title: SRv6 Behaviors and Payload Size
sections.content:
With an MPLS PSN, a VPWS label does the demultiplexing. With SRv6, an SRv6 service SID does it, with rules from RFC 9252 and either full IPv6 SIDs from RFC 8986 or compressed SIDs from RFC 9800.

The RFC defines two new encapsulation behaviors, H.Encaps.L1 and H.Encaps.L1.Red, which wrap the frame from the IWF in an IPv6 packet. The next header of the SRH or last extension header MUST be 147. It also defines three endpoint behaviors, End.DX1 and its NEXT-CSID and REPLACE-CSID variants. At the endpoint, if the upper-layer header type is 147, the outer IPv6 header and extension headers are removed and the frame goes to the IWF.

The payload size is fixed when the VPWS is set up, is the same in both directions and never changes. Every implementation MUST support the default of 1024 bytes, and the smallest supported size is 64 bytes. In the basic payload, bits are packed from most to least significant without regard to structure. In the byte-aligned payload, bytes keep their order and the size MUST be a whole number of bytes.
sections.plainLanguage: All packages on one line are the same size, chosen when the line is set up. The usual size is 1024 bytes.

sections.title: How the Two Ends Behave
sections.content:
The sending IWF cuts the data into equal payloads, adds the control word, RTP header and demultiplexing headers, and sets L when the attachment circuit has a fault and R when its own receive side is losing packets.

The receiving IWF MUST keep a de-jitter buffer, whose size SHOULD be configurable for the expected packet delay variation. It SHOULD use the control word sequence number to find lost and misordered packets. If it cannot reorder, it MUST drop misordered packets. A lost payload MUST be replaced with an equal amount of replacement data, and every implementation MUST support 0xAA by default, whose alternating bits keep the clock going and avoid invalid sync headers in 64B/66B services.

When a circuit comes up, the IWF fills the buffer to a preconfigured level (typically 50% of the buffer) before streaming out. If packets are lost for a preconfigured time (default 1 millisecond), it enters the PLOS state. If packet loss rate stays above a signal-degrade threshold (default 15%) for a configurable number of consecutive 1-second intervals (2 to 10, default 7), it enters the DEG state. While PLOS is declared, the NSP injects the service's downstream fault signal, or MAY disable its transmitter if none exists.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver waits until it has a small pile of packages before it starts, so a late one does not cause a gap. If one never shows up, it fills the hole with a harmless pattern.

sections.title: Monitoring, QoS and Congestion
sections.content:
Performance monitoring is defined with near-end counters: PLE Errored Seconds (ES-PLE), Severely Errored Seconds (SES-PLE) and Unavailable Seconds (UAS-PLE). A second with a lost packet or a PLOS or DEG defect is an ES-PLE. A second with a loss rate above 15% or a PLOS or DEG defect is an SES-PLE. Unavailability starts and ends after a configurable number of consecutive seconds, default 10. Monitoring data and fault information MUST be available through the management interface and SHOULD be provided by a YANG data model, which is out of scope.

PLE pseudowires are inelastic constant bit rate flows that cannot respond to congestion in a TCP-friendly manner and are sensitive to jitter, loss and reordering. The network therefore has to supply low jitter and low loss, for example with Diffserv and Expedited Forwarding, traffic-engineered paths with bandwidth reservation, or over-provisioning.
sections.plainLanguage: The line keeps a scoreboard of bad seconds. Since the traffic cannot slow down when the road is busy, the road itself has to be kept clear.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content:
PLE neither improves nor weakens the security of the underlying PSN and relies on it for encryption, integrity and authentication where needed. The PSN is assumed to be trusted and secure, and attackers who inject spoofed packets could easily disrupt the service, so best practices for isolating the PSN MUST be followed. Random initial sequence numbers make known-plaintext attacks harder, and checking the RTP SSRC or payload type can catch misconnections and some denial-of-service attacks.

IANA assigned decimal 147, keyword BIT-EMU, Bit-stream Emulation, as an IP protocol number and IPv6 extension header value. It also assigned three SRv6 endpoint behavior values: 158 (End.DX1), 159 (with NEXT-CSID) and 160 (with REPLACE-CSID).
sections.plainLanguage: The private line is only as safe as the shared network under it. Keep strangers off that network and the line stays safe.
